title: OpenAI Says GPT-6 Can Design Proteins Without Specialized Biology Models
summary: OpenAI says GPT-6 can design proteins without specialized biology models
detailed: OpenAI announced that its GPT-6 family of models can design new protein structures and amino acid sequences using reasoning and general-purpose coding tools instead of purpose-built biology models.
In lab experiments with research partner Onava, proteins designed by GPT-6.2 showed binding across multiple targets, including a 10.9% hit rate on minibinders and 70% on antibody binding loops.
Across generations, GPT-6.2 increased its mean DockQ score for antibody binding prediction to 0.57 and improved ranking mutations by effect on stability over specialized model ESM2-650M.
Whole-structure prediction from sequence alone remained a weak point, with the latest internal model averaging a TM-score of 0.38 compared to ESMFold2 at 0.93.
sentences: OpenAI's GPT-6 family of models can design new protein structures and amino acid sequences on its own, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools rather than calling on purpose-built biology models, the company said in a preprint published on November 24, 2026.

The paper, titled "GPT-6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models," describes a system that researchers can steer in plain language, specifying where a designed protein should attach to its target and what shape it should take.
OpenAI said the work points toward a future in which scientists describe the molecule they want and let a general-purpose model propose candidates for laboratory testing.

"Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities," the company said, adding that it could guide its models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein.
The results land in a field where protein design has been dominated by narrow, task-specific systems such as RFdiffusion for generating backbones and ProteinMPNN for assigning sequences.
OpenAI's central claim is that a single large language model can handle much of that work while accepting new kinds of instructions without retraining.
OpenAI worked with research partner Onava to put some of the designs into physical form.
Proteins built from structures designed by a pre-release version of GPT-6.2 showed evidence of binding across five targets.

In a separate set of experiments, GPT-6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies, and many of the redesigned proteins retained their ability to bind the original targets.
In the first lab experiment, the team tested 322 minibinders against five targets and found 35, or 10.9%, that tested positive for binding.
The hits broke down as 18 for IL-17A, 8 for VEGF-A, 5 for PD-L1, 3 for IL-7Rα and 1 for TrkA.

The company acknowledged that the original RFdiffusion study reported higher hit rates, but said the rates depend heavily on how strictly designs are filtered before lab validation and on how binding is defined.
A second experiment asked GPT-6.2 to propose sequences for three-dimensional structures of known minibinders while withholding the original sequences.
Initial lab screens showed binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%) and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%).
The proposed sequences often differed substantially from the originals, with a median divergence of 50% for VEGF-A, 43% for MDM2 and 15% for PD-1.
The most telling results came from unpublished structures.

Given a previously unseen PD-L1 minibinder shape, the model produced two sequences that differed from the original at 52 and 58 of 90 positions and from each other at 44 positions, and both showed signs of binding.
OpenAI said that outcome is strong evidence the capability extends beyond memorization.
In antibody work, the model redesigned binding loops on six small antibodies targeting IL-4Rα, and 128 of 182 designs (70%) showed signs of binding.
When asked to alter roughly half the amino acids in three binding loops of five therapeutic antibodies, 179 of 272 fragments (66%) bound to their original targets, PD-1 or PD-L1.
Across a range of computational benchmarks, OpenAI's latest internal model matched or beat specialized tools on most tasks.

The models also improved steadily across generations at predicting where an antibody binds.
With side-chain detail hidden, the mean DockQ score rose from about 0.05 for GPT-5.6 to 0.28 for GPT-6, 0.57 for GPT-6.2 and 0.81 for the latest internal model.

On ranking mutations by their effect on protein stability, the rank correlation climbed from 0.41 to 0.66 over the same generations, beating the specialized model ESM2-650M on all four public datasets tested.
OpenAI was explicit that whole-structure prediction remains a weak point.
Asked to predict how a chain folds from its sequence alone, the latest internal model averaged a TM-score of 0.38, up from 0.16 for GPT-5.6 and 0.26 for GPT-6.2, but far behind ESMFold2 at 0.93.
The design pipeline also leaned on outside tools.

Specialized structure-prediction models including Boltz-2, OpenDDE and ESMFold2 filtered candidates, while SolubleMPNN supplied sequences for the first minibinder experiment and ProteinMPNN and ESMFold were used in the motif-scaffolding tests.
OpenAI said the results therefore do not yet show that its models can generate de novo minibinders end-to-end without help.

"Binding is only one step toward a useful research tool or medicine," the company said, noting that specificity, stability and biological activity still need to be established, along with safety and efficacy for therapeutic use.
It also cautioned that unusually high scores on some structure-to-sequence benchmarks may partly reflect memorization or patterns in how the test structures were generated.
The findings, if they hold up, would mark a shift in how computational biology tools are built and sold.

Much of the sector's value rests on specialized models that require expert users to coordinate inputs and constraints, and OpenAI's pitch is that a general model can absorb new requirements through prompting alone.
That could lower the barrier for research teams without structural biology expertise, while pressuring vendors of niche design software.
For drugmakers, the more immediate question is whether machine-designed proteins survive contact with the lab.
A 10.9% binding rate in the first experiment is a starting point rather than a validated pipeline, and turning binders into manufacturable, selective molecules remains the harder problem.

OpenAI laid out three priorities for the next phase: finding minibinders for targets where attempts have so far failed, designing for biological effects after binding such as killing cancer cells, and extending the approach to molecules that hit multiple targets, RNA, small molecules and PROTACs.
The company also said it is assessing biosecurity risks under its Preparedness Framework, acknowledging that the same capabilities that help design new medicines could be misused.
The company's stated end goal is to shorten each round of design so that fewer lab-test cycles are needed to reach a working protein.
"Ultimately, we envision enabling scientists to design proteins and molecules simply by prompting our models in natural language," it said.
